The study of non-overlapping codes (also called strongly regular codes, cross-bifix-free codes) is motivated by applications for synchronization in communications, and it goes back to the 1950s. A code S\subseteq\cup_{n\geq 2}\mathbb{Z}_{q}^{n} is called non-overlapping if two conditions hold: 1) the prefix of each codeword is not a suffix of any codeword in S, including itself; 2) for all distinct codewords \mathbf{u,v}\in S, \mathbf{u} does not contain \mathbf{v} as a subword. If all codewords in S have the same length n, the second condition is satisfied automatically, and then S is called a fixed-length non-overlapping code; if not, it is called a variable-length non-overlapping code.

Research on non-overlapping codes mostly focuses on deriving bounds on their cardinality in terms of parameters like the code length n and the alphabet size q, and also on constructing non-overlapping codes of large size that are close to the bounds. Levenshtein gave the first construction, and it was rediscovered later. Recently non-overlapping codes have found important applications in DNA storage systems. More constructions of fixed-length non-overlapping codes can be found in other works. There is also a series of recent advances on non-overlapping codes and their extensions.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The study of non-overlapping codes (also called strongly regular codes, cross-bifix-free codes) is motivated by applications for synchronization in communications, and it goes back to the 1950s. A code S\subseteq\cup_{n\geq 2}\mathbb{Z}_{q}^{n} is called non-overlapping if two conditions hold: 1) the prefix of each codeword is not a suffix of any codeword in S, including itself; 2) for all distinct codewords \mathbf{u,v}\in S, \mathbf{u} does not contain \mathbf{v} as a subword. If all codewords in S have the same length n, the second condition is satisfied automatically, and then S is called a fixed-length non-overlapping code; if not, it is called a variable-length non-overlapping code.

Research on non-overlapping codes mostly focuses on deriving bounds on their cardinality in terms of parameters like the code length n and the alphabet size q, and also on constructing non-overlapping codes of large size that are close to the bounds. Levenshtein gave the first construction, and it was rediscovered later. Recently non-overlapping codes have found important applications in DNA storage systems. More constructions of fixed-length non-overlapping codes can be found in other works. There is also a series of recent advances on non-overlapping codes and their extensions.

Let C(n,q) be the maximum size of fixed-length non-overlapping codes over an alphabet of size q. The best-known upper bound was given by Levenshtein and is

Blackburn then showed that this bound is tight if n divides q. In 2017 Bilotta defined variable-length non-overlapping codes and gave a binary construction that extends Levenshtein’s construction. Later the authors proposed a generating functions approach to construct q -ary non-overlapping codes for both the fixed-length and the variable-length case. For the maximum size of variable-length non-overlapping codes, unlike the fixed-length case, it seems hard to find a direct upper bound, and only recursive bounds have been reported. More precisely, let S\subseteq\cup_{i=m}^{n}\mathbb{Z}_{q}^{i} be a variable-length non-overlapping code over \mathbb{Z}_{q}=\{0,1,\ldots,q-1\}, an alphabet of size q, and let S_{i}=S\cap\mathbb{Z}_{q}^{i} be the set of codewords of length i in S for m\leq i\leq n. A direct way to bound S is to add up all the values of |S_{i}|, which gives the trivial bound |S|\leq\sum_{i=m}^{n}C(i,q). Intuitively this suggests that a variable-length non-overlapping code with codeword length at most n might contain more codewords than a fixed-length non-overlapping code with code length n. As far as the authors know, deriving a nontrivial direct bound on the cardinality of variable-length non-overlapping codes is still an open problem.

In this paper we first establish a new link between variable-length and fixed-length non-overlapping codes, by showing that a variable-length non-overlapping code can always be extended to a fixed-length non-overlapping code in a systematic way. This means the cardinality of variable-length non-overlapping codes can be upper bounded by that of fixed-length non-overlapping codes. We also look at the average length of codewords in variable-length non-overlapping codes, and we prove that it is lower bounded by \lceil\log_{q}\tilde{C}\rceil, where \tilde{C} is the cardinality of q -ary variable-length non-overlapping codes of length up to n.

The rest of the paper is organized like this. Section 2 introduces some notations and definitions. Section 3 first gives a systematic way to extend variable-length non-overlapping codes to fixed-length ones, and then bounds the cardinality of variable-length non-overlapping codes. Section 4 gives results on the minimum average length of codewords in variable-length non-overlapping codes. Section 5 concludes the paper.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Motivated by applications for synchronization in communications, the study of non-overlapping codes (also called strongly regular codes, cross-bifix-free codes) dates back to the 1950s [1]. A code S\subseteq\cup_{n\geq 2}\mathbb{Z}_{q}^{n} is called non-overlapping if the following two conditions are satisfied: 1) the prefix of each codeword is not a suffix of any codeword in S, including itself; 2) for all distinct codewords \mathbf{u,v}\in S, \mathbf{u} does not contain \mathbf{v} as a subword. If all codewords in S have the same length n, the second condition is automatically satisfied, and S is then called a fixed-length non-overlapping code; otherwise, it is called a variable-length non-overlapping code.

The study of non-overlapping codes mainly focuses on deriving bounds on their cardinality with respect to parameters including the code length n and the alphabet size q, and on constructing non-overlapping codes of large size close to these bounds. The first construction was given by Levenshtein [2,3,4], and was later rediscovered in [5,6,7]. Recently, non-overlapping codes have found important applications in DNA storage systems [8,9]. For further constructions of fixed-length non-overlapping codes, see, for example, [10,11,12,13,14]. We also refer to [15,16,17,18,19] for a series of recent advances in non-overlapping codes and their extensions.

Denote by C(n,q) the maximum size of fixed-length non-overlapping codes over an alphabet of size q. The best-known upper bound, given by Levenshtein [3], is

Blackburn [12] further showed that this bound is tight if n divides q. In 2017, Bilotta [20] defined variable-length non-overlapping codes and gave a binary construction by extending Levenshtein’s construction. Later, the authors [15] proposed a generating functions approach to constructing q -ary non-overlapping codes for both the fixed-length and variable-length cases. Unlike the fixed-length case, it seems difficult to find a direct upper bound on the maximum size of variable-length non-overlapping codes, and only recursive bounds have been reported [20,15]. More precisely, let S\subseteq\cup_{i=m}^{n}\mathbb{Z}_{q}^{i} denote a variable-length non-overlapping code over \mathbb{Z}_{q}=\{0,1,\ldots,q-1\}, an alphabet of size q, and let S_{i}=S\cap\mathbb{Z}_{q}^{i} denote the set of codewords of length i in S for m\leq i\leq n. One direct way to bound S is to sum up all the values of |S_{i}|, which leads to the trivial bound |S|\leq\sum_{i=m}^{n}C(i,q) [20]. Intuitively, this suggests that a variable-length non-overlapping code with codeword length at most n may contain more codewords than a fixed-length non-overlapping code with code length n. To the best of the authors' knowledge, deriving a nontrivial direct bound on the cardinality of variable-length non-overlapping codes remains an open problem.

In this paper, we first establish a new link between variable-length and fixed-length non-overlapping codes by showing that a variable-length non-overlapping code can always be extended to a fixed-length one in a systematic way. The cardinality of variable-length non-overlapping codes can therefore be upper bounded by that of fixed-length non-overlapping codes. Furthermore, we investigate the average length of codewords in variable-length non-overlapping codes, and prove that it is lower bounded by \lceil\log_{q}\tilde{C}\rceil, where \tilde{C} denotes the cardinality of q -ary variable-length non-overlapping codes of length up to n.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces some notations and definitions. In Section 3, we first give a systematic way to extend variable-length non-overlapping codes to fixed-length ones, and then bound the cardinality of variable-length non-overlapping codes. Section 4 provides results on the minimum average length of codewords in variable-length non-overlapping codes. Finally, Section 5 concludes the paper.
